gap: No result ChatGPT got states that an inverter wired into an RV's AC panel must switch its neutral-to-ground bond: the bond is closed while inverting and opened before shore power passes through. That switching is what the transfer relay in an inverter/charger does (Renogy's REGO 'integrated transfer relay with neutral ground bonding'; Victron's ground relay H, which 'automatically connects the Neutral output to the chassis if no external AC supply is available' and opens 'before the input safety relay closes').
standout_why: I opened both pages ChatGPT cited. Victron's 'How to Size a Solar System for Your RV' (2026-05-04) covers Wh-to-Ah sizing and says only that you need 'correctly sized solar cables, cable lugs, DC fuses'. It says nothing about neutral-ground bonding, a ground relay, a transfer switch or GFCI. The text I could read from Renogy's 'RV Inverter Installation Guide' was only 6,855 characters, mostly site navigation, and also says nothing about bonding or transfer behaviour. rvtime.com would not load (SSL certificate error), and the Victron RV brochure PDF came back as unreadable compressed streams, so I couldn't check those two. Nothing I could read explains why a whole-coach install needs bond switching. ChatGPT's answer only lists 'Transfer switch' as a feature on card 1.
decides: It splits ChatGPT's three cards by what the shopper plans to do. If the inverter will feed the RV's existing outlets and panel alongside shore power, the shopper needs a unit whose transfer relay switches the N-G bond. The Renogy REGO 3000W inverter/charger states this on its product page, which supports card 3 (now $989.99 on renogy.com, not the $949 ChatGPT showed). If the shopper only plugs loads into the inverter's own outlets, bond switching doesn't come into play, and the cheaper standalone units (card 1 or 2) work. I couldn't confirm whether the standalone 3000W (P2) has a fixed internal bond, so the page shouldn't say it does.
